page: Microsoft Azure E20s_v7 is a memory-optimized virtual machine belonging to the Esv7 family, powered by the Microsoft Hyper-V hypervisor. It features 20 dedicated vCPUs mapped to 10 physical cores of an Intel Xeon 6973P-C processor operating at 4.2 GHz. The x86_64 architecture includes 160.0 GB of system memory, providing a high memory-to-vCPU ratio of 8.0 GB per vCPU. The processor is equipped with a 480 MB L3 cache, 2 MB L2 cache, and 48 KB L1d cache, alongside advanced instruction sets such as AVX-512 and Intel Advanced Matrix Extensions (AMX) for accelerated matrix operations.

This server configuration does not include local ephemeral storage, meaning all storage requirements must be met via external Premium Storage options. It also does not include complimentary public IPv4 addresses or onboard GPU accelerators. The absence of local storage and dedicated graphics hardware represents a clear tradeoff, positioning this instance primarily for workloads that rely on network-attached storage and CPU-bound processing.

Benchmark data indicates average performance across most standard compute and memory metrics, with a stress-ng single-core score of 2232.95 and a multi-core score of 20536.75. However, single-threaded operations show strong efficiency, with gzip compression reaching 35.43 GB/sec and bzip3 decompression at 14.68 GB/sec, both placing in the top 25%. Large block memory bandwidth reads and writes are measured at 139.09 GB/sec and 57.2 GB/sec respectively. Notably, the instance achieves top-tier performance in small-model LLM text generation, processing 364.6 tokens per second with a 135M parameter model, aided by Intel AMX instruction support.

From a cost-efficiency perspective, the E20s_v7 offers a high-density memory profile relative to its vCPU count, making it a viable option for memory-intensive workloads that do not require massive parallel compute scaling. The combination of 160 GB of RAM, dedicated Intel Xeon cores, and AMX instructions makes this server suitable for relational database hosting, in-memory caching systems like Redis, enterprise resource planning applications, and CPU-based machine learning inference.
